section.title: Laws of Compassion
section.sectionRationale: This chapter gathers laws that protect the economically vulnerable, debtors, day laborers, widows, orphans, and foreigners, showing that Israel's remembrance of its own slavery in Egypt must translate into concrete compassion, not mere sentiment.
section.thesis: Because Israel was itself once a vulnerable, oppressed people redeemed by the LORD, this chapter requires concrete compassion toward debtors, day laborers, the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow, refusing to let poverty or vulnerability become an excuse for exploitation.
section.frameNote: Seven movements: the certificate of divorce and its limits; mercy exemptions and warnings for the newly married, the millstone, kidnapping, and skin disease; the dignity of the debtor; fair wages for the hired poor; individual responsibility for one's own sin; justice for the foreigner, fatherless, and widow; and gleaning laws that leave a share of the harvest for the poor.

units.label: A certificate of divorce
units.note: regulating, not commending, an existing practice

verses.text: If a man marries a woman, but she becomes displeasing to him because he finds some indecency in her, he may write her a certificate of divorce, hand it to her, and send her away from his house.
If, after leaving his house, she goes and becomes another man's wife,
and the second man hates her, writes her a certificate of divorce, hands it to her, and sends her away from his house, or if he dies,

then the husband who divorced her first may not remarry her after she has been defiled, for that is an abomination to the LORD. You must not bring sin upon the land that the LORD your God is giving you as an inheritance.

units.label: Mercy exemptions and warnings
units.note: the newlywed, the millstone, kidnapping, skin disease

verses.text: If a man is newly married, he must not be sent to war or be pressed into any duty. For one year he is free to stay at home and bring joy to the wife he has married.
Do not take a pair of millstones or even an upper millstone as security for a debt, because that would be taking one's livelihood as security.
If a man is caught kidnapping one of his Israelite brothers, whether he treats him as a slave or sells him, the kidnapper must die. So you must purge the evil from among you.
In cases of infectious skin diseases, be careful to diligently follow everything the Levitical priests instruct you. Be careful to do as I have commanded them.
Remember what the LORD your God did to Miriam on the journey after you came out of Egypt.

units.label: The dignity of the debtor
units.note: a pledge must not humiliate the poor

verses.text: When you lend anything to your neighbor, do not enter his house to collect {{mashkon|security}}.
You are to stand outside while the man to whom you are lending brings the security out to you.
If he is a poor man, you must not go to sleep with the security in your possession;
be sure to return it to him by sunset, so that he may sleep in his own cloak and bless you, and this will be credited to you as {{tzedaqah|righteousness}} before the LORD your God.

units.label: Fair wages, not oppression
units.note: the hired hand who is poor and needy

verses.text: Do not oppress a hired hand who is poor and needy, whether he is a brother or a foreigner residing in one of your towns.
You are to pay his wages each day before sunset, because he is poor and depends on them. Otherwise he may cry out to the LORD against you, and you will be guilty of sin.

units.label: Each bears his own guilt
units.note: no punishing children for a father's sin, or the reverse

verses.text: Fathers shall not be put to death for their children, nor children for their fathers; each is to die for his own sin.

units.label: Justice for the vulnerable
units.note: remember you were slaves in Egypt

verses.text: Do not deny justice to the {{ger|foreigner}} or the fatherless, and do not take a widow's cloak as security.
Remember that you were slaves in Egypt, and the LORD your God redeemed you from that place. Therefore I am commanding you to do this.

units.label: Gleaning for the poor
units.note: a share of every harvest left behind

verses.text: If you are harvesting in your field and forget a sheaf there, do not go back to get it. It is to be left for the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow, so that the LORD your God may bless you in all the work of your hands.
When you beat the olives from your trees, you must not go over the branches again. What remains will be for the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow.
When you gather the grapes of your vineyard, you must not go over the vines again. What remains will be for the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow.
Remember that you were slaves in the land of Egypt. Therefore I am commanding you to do this.

mashkon.gloss: Pledge, security taken for a loan. The law protects the poor debtor's dignity and basic needs, requiring the pledge be returned by nightfall if he needs it to sleep.

tzedaqah.gloss: Righteousness. Returning a poor man's cloak pledge by nightfall 'will be credited to you as righteousness before the LORD your God,' tying practical, costly compassion directly to righteousness before God.

ger.gloss: Sojourner, resident foreigner. Paired repeatedly with the fatherless and the widow as among the most vulnerable in Israel's society, whom the LORD commands His people to actively provide for and defend.

basic.context: This chapter moves through a series of laws protecting the vulnerable: limits on divorce and remarriage, a year's exemption from military and civic duty for a newly married man, protection of a poor debtor's dignity and basic needs, prompt fair wages for the hired poor, individual rather than family guilt, justice for the foreigner, fatherless, and widow, and gleaning laws that leave part of every harvest for the poor, all grounded in Israel's own memory of slavery in Egypt.
basic.hermeneutics: These specific old covenant provisions, the divorce certificate, security pledges, gleaning, describe Israel's particular economic and legal setting, not a direct legal code for today, yet the repeated command to 'remember that you were slaves in Egypt' as the ground for compassion carries forward as an enduring principle for how God's redeemed people are to treat the vulnerable.
basic.originalLanguages: The law protects the poor debtor's mashkon, pledge or security, requiring its return by nightfall if he needs it to sleep, calling this act of compassion tzedaqah, righteousness, before the LORD. The recurring triad of the ger, foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow names Israel's most vulnerable, who are to receive active justice, not neglect.
basic.typology: Israel's gleaning laws, deliberately leaving a share of the harvest unharvested for the poor, become the very provision that brings Ruth the Moabite widow into Boaz's field and, eventually, into the line of King David and of Christ.
basic.christ: Ruth 2 shows the gleaning law of this chapter working exactly as intended: a poor foreign widow finds provision and, ultimately, redemption through Boaz, a picture of Christ our kinsman-redeemer who gathers in the outsider and the destitute.
basic.god: God grounds Israel's compassion not in sentiment but in memory: 'remember that you were slaves in Egypt, and the LORD your God redeemed you from that place,' verses 18 and 22. His own redeeming character becomes the reason His people must show mercy to those as vulnerable as they once were.
basic.crossReferences: Ruth 2:1-23 shows gleaning law in action for a poor Moabite widow. Matthew 19:8 has Jesus explain that Moses permitted divorce because of hardness of heart, not as God's original design. Leviticus 19:9-10 gives the parallel gleaning command. James 5:4 warns against withholding a laborer's wages.
basic.oneStory: The compassion commanded here, rooted in Israel's own redemption from slavery, anticipates the far greater compassion of Christ, who gathers in the foreigner, the widow, and the poor, and redeems His people not from Egypt but from sin itself.

context.literary:
This chapter gathers seven units unified less by subject matter than by a single concern, protecting whoever is most easily overlooked in a household or a harvest. It opens with a difficult, negatively framed case, the certificate of divorce and its limits, and closes with a positive command repeated almost verbatim three times, it is to be left for the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow, in verses 19, 20, and 21. The chapter's movement, from a restriction guarding against one specific abuse to a near liturgical refrain of generosity, mirrors its own argument, the law does not merely forbid harm, it actively builds provision for the vulnerable into ordinary life.

The middle section, verses 5 to 16, alternates mercy exemptions, a newlywed freed from war, a debtor's pledge protected, with sober warnings, kidnapping punished by death, skin disease requiring strict priestly diligence, Miriam remembered as a warning. Verse 16's single-sentence principle of individual responsibility, fathers shall not be put to death for their children, sits almost like a hinge in the middle of this section, everything before it concerns protecting an individual from being crushed by someone else's power, a creditor, a kidnapper, a communal grudge, and everything after it concerns an individual's own duty toward other vulnerable individuals, a hired worker, a foreigner, a fatherless child, a widow.

The chapter closes its final three units, verses 17-18 and 19-22, around a single refrain, remember that you were slaves in Egypt, stated explicitly at both ends of the unit, functioning as the chapter's own theological climax, the reason finally given out loud for a concern that has quietly shaped every law before it.
context.historical:
The certificate of divorce, sefer keritut, functioned in the ancient world partly as protection for the woman herself, documented proof that her marriage had been legally ended and that she was therefore free to remarry without being accused of adultery, which is why this law regulates the procedure rather than banning it outright. The specific abuse it targets, a first husband reclaiming a wife who has since married and been widowed or divorced again, likely guarded against a man profiting from repeated arrangements at his former wife's expense.

The newlywed's year long exemption from military service and civic duty, verse 5, is unusual set against surrounding warfare cultures, which typically conscripted broadly without domestic exception, and it reflects a striking prioritization of ordinary marital joy over even the urgent demands of national defense.

The millstone law, verse 6, reflects daily reality rather than abstract principle, a household ground its own grain fresh each day with a hand mill, so taking either stone as security left a family unable to make bread that day, which is precisely the reasoning the law itself states, that would be taking one's livelihood as security.

The requirement that a creditor stand outside and let the debtor bring out his own pledge, verses 10 to 11, is an unusual restraint on a creditor's power in any ancient economy, where pledge taking practices ranged from routine to genuinely abusive, protecting a poor household's privacy and dignity even in the act of settling a legitimate debt. And the gleaning provisions of verses 19 to 21 describe a real, structural safety net rather than an ideal never put into practice, as the book of Ruth later shows it actually functioning for one particular widow.
context.canonical:
Ruth 2 shows this chapter's gleaning law operating exactly as written, and then exceeding it, Boaz does not merely permit Ruth to glean, he instructs his workers to pull grain out for her on purpose, going beyond the law's own minimum requirement, Ruth 2:15-16. The individual responsibility principle of verse 16 is cited by name centuries later, when King Amaziah spares the children of his father's assassins, explicitly acting according to what is written in the Book of the Law of Moses, 2 Kings 14:6, a rare, recorded instance of a king obeying this precise text word for word.

The certificate of divorce reappears in an unexpected register in Jeremiah, where the LORD describes His own relationship with faithless Israel using this chapter's exact legal language, I gave her a certificate of divorce and sent her away, Jeremiah 3:8, an image that makes Israel's covenant unfaithfulness concrete by borrowing the very procedure this law regulates.

Jesus takes up the same law directly in His teaching on divorce, explaining that Moses permitted it because of hardness of heart, not because it reflected marriage as God designed it in Genesis 2, Matthew 19:3-9, reaching back past this chapter's concession to the creation account it was never meant to replace. And the chapter's twice repeated ground for compassion, remember that you were slaves in Egypt, echoes a refrain that runs throughout Deuteronomy, appearing also at 5:15, 15:15, and 16:12, showing this is not a passing sentiment but the settled theological basis Moses gives, again and again, for how Israel is to treat the vulnerable.

hermeneutics.authorIntent: Moses wants Israel's economic and social practice to embody the character of the God who redeemed them from slavery, so that every provision in this chapter functions as applied memory. A divorced woman's status is protected, a newlywed is given a year of undistracted joy, a debtor's dignity is guarded even while a legitimate debt is collected, a poor laborer is paid before he has to wonder whether he will be, guilt is assigned to the person who commits a sin rather than spread across a family, and a share of every harvest is guaranteed in advance to the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow. None of this is presented as optional kindness left to individual generosity, Moses intends it as the ordinary, structural shape covenant life takes for a people who once needed exactly this kind of mercy and did not receive it in Egypt.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription: The specific mechanics here, the certificate procedure, the exact boundaries of gleaning, the precise timing of a daily wage, describe Israel's particular ancient economy and legal system and are not a direct legal code for today. Jesus himself models how later revelation can reinterpret Mosaic case law without discarding its underlying wisdom, reading the divorce provision in Matthew 19:8 as a concession to hardness of heart rather than marriage as God intended it. What carries forward as an enduring principle is not any specific dollar amount or harvest boundary but the pattern itself, a people redeemed by God are to build structural, guaranteed provision for the vulnerable into their ordinary economic life rather than leaving generosity to occasional charity or individual discretion.

debates.question: How should Christians understand the divorce certificate law of verses 1-4 in light of Jesus' teaching?

views.label: A concession regulating an already existing practice
views.case: Jesus explicitly says in Matthew 19:8 that Moses permitted divorce because your hearts were hard, not because it reflected God's original design in creation, so this law limits and regulates divorce's abuse rather than commanding or endorsing the practice itself.

views.label: A law protecting a specific vulnerable party from further exploitation
views.case: The main concern of the passage is not a general theology of divorce but forbidding remarriage to the first husband once the woman has married another man, a targeted protection against one particular abuse, likely guarding against a man profiting from repeated divorce and remarriage at his former wife's expense.

debates.bearing: Both readings agree this text regulates a difficult, already existing reality rather than establishing or commending divorce, and neither treats it as God's design for marriage, which Jesus locates instead in Genesis 2.

debates.question: What does ervat davar, rendered some indecency, in verse 1 mean?

views.label: A narrow reference to serious sexual sin
views.case: The word ervah is used elsewhere in the Torah specifically for sexual immorality and forbidden unions, Leviticus 18 and 20, so on this reading the grounds for the certificate described here were already understood as fairly serious rather than trivial.

views.label: A broader, deliberately ambiguous phrase
views.case: Later Jewish interpretation split sharply over the phrase's breadth, one reading treating it narrowly as serious wrongdoing and another reading it as covering nearly any cause of a husband's displeasure, an ambiguity that likely reflects how loosely the practice had already come to be applied by the time of Jesus.

debates.bearing: Jesus does not settle the ancient debate over the phrase's precise scope, He goes further back, past the concession itself, to Genesis 2's design for marriage, and calls His hearers to that far higher standard rather than to the most permissive available reading of Moses.

study.originalLanguages:
Verses 1 and 3 call the document a man gives his wife a sefer keritut, literally a document of cutting off, built on karat, the same verb Israel uses when it cuts a covenant, karat berit. The pairing is almost ironic, the very verb that describes binding a relationship together in covenant is here used for a document that formally cuts one apart, as if the law itself marks divorce as covenant language turned against its own purpose.

The indecency that grounds the certificate in verse 1 is ervat davar, literally the nakedness of a matter, an unusually vague construct phrase for a law with such serious consequences. Ervah elsewhere in the Torah names specific forbidden sexual unions, Leviticus 18 and 20, which argues for a narrower sense here, yet the addition of davar, an all-purpose word for thing or matter, broadens what could otherwise be a precise legal term into something genuinely ambiguous, a vagueness later interpreters would stretch in very different directions.

Verse 4 calls remarriage after this sequence to'evah, an abomination, the same strong word this collection of laws uses for cross-dressing (22:5) and for bringing a prostitute's wages into the LORD's house (23:18). Across three consecutive chapters the word marks out things Israel's covenant life must simply refuse to accommodate, regardless of how common or legally arranged they might otherwise appear.

The triad ger, yathom, almanah, foreigner, fatherless, and widow, verse 17 and again in verses 19 to 21, is one of the most repeated formulas in Deuteronomy, compare 10:18, 14:29, 16:11, 16:14, 26:12-13, naming Israel's three characteristic categories of the powerless, those without land, without a father's protection, and without a husband's provision. Naming all three together, rather than reaching for a single general word for the poor, keeps the law specific about exactly who is most easily overlooked.

Finally, verse 19 turns an ordinary human failure into a built-in provision, if you forget a sheaf, using shakhach, the common verb for forgetting, and simply commands, do not go back to get it. The law does not require perfect memory or deliberate charity in the moment, it treats an honest mistake most farmers would want to correct as itself already belonging to the poor, so that even imperfect obedience still leaves something behind for the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow.

typology.type: Gleaning left for the foreigner, fatherless, and widow, Deuteronomy 24:19-21
typology.fulfillment: Boaz not only allows Ruth to glean, he tells his workers to pull grain out for her on purpose, going beyond what this law required, Ruth 2:15-16, and the child born from their marriage becomes King David's grandfather. The law's floor of provision becomes, in Ruth's story, the occasion for a kinsman redeemer's deliberate generosity and, through it, the Messiah's own family line. The type is real but partial, Boaz redeems one widow's field and future, Christ redeems a people who, like Ruth, had no claim of their own to make on Him at all.

typology.type: Prompt payment of the poor hired worker, Deuteronomy 24:14-15
typology.fulfillment: The law will not let a wage owed to someone who depends on it that same day wait until it is convenient for the employer. James warns landowners centuries later in almost identical terms, that withheld wages cry out and have reached the ears of the Lord of Hosts, James 5:4, the same picture of a wronged worker's cry the law already assumed would reach God. Jesus states the positive principle behind both texts, the worker is worthy of his wages, Luke 10:7, a standard His own sent-out disciples are told to expect kept, not merely hoped for.

Centuries later Jeremiah has the LORD apply this very language to Himself, describing faithless Israel and saying, I gave her a certificate of divorce and sent her away, Jeremiah 3:8, an astonishing admission that Israel's own unfaithfulness had brought about what this law regulates. Yet the LORD keeps pursuing her even after the certificate, and the New Testament describes a covenant in Christ that, unlike a certificate of cutting off, cannot be revoked, sealed instead by a promise never to leave or forsake, Hebrews 13:5. The type is a contrast more than a correspondence, a document that legally ends a marriage answered by a covenant nothing can end.

typology.type: The newly married man freed for a year of joy, Deuteronomy 24:5
typology.fulfillment: Israel's ordinary demands, even war itself, give way for a full year so a bridegroom can devote himself to his wife. Jesus uses the same logic when questioned about fasting, how can the guests of the bridegroom mourn while he is with them, Matthew 9:15, treating a wedding's joy as something that rightly suspends the usual rhythms of duty and grief. Revelation completes the picture with the marriage of the Lamb, where the bride is finally, permanently ready, Revelation 19:7-9, the ordinary joy this law protects for one year becoming, in Christ, a joy with no end fixed to it at all.

study.christ:
This chapter's road to Christ runs mostly through contrast and pattern rather than direct promise, but the contrasts are pointed. The certificate of divorce in verses 1 to 4 legally, permanently cuts a marriage apart, sefer keritut, literally a document of cutting off, built ironically on the same root Israel uses for cutting a covenant. Centuries later Jeremiah has the LORD apply this very language to Himself, I gave her a certificate of divorce, describing faithless Israel, Jeremiah 3:8. And yet the LORD does not actually walk away, the rest of Jeremiah is full of pursuit and promise. The New Testament shows where that pursuit finally lands, a covenant sealed by Christ that, unlike any human certificate, cannot be cut off, never will I leave you or forsake you, Hebrews 13:5, and a new covenant written on the heart rather than on a scroll that can be handed over and walked away from, Jeremiah 31:31-34.

The gleaning laws of verses 19 to 21 open just as directly onto Christ, though through one particular story. Boaz does not merely permit Ruth, a poor Moabite widow, to glean as the law required, he tells his workers to pull grain from the bundles on purpose for her, Ruth 2:15-16, generosity that goes beyond the law's floor. Ruth's son becomes the grandfather of David, and the line runs on to Jesus, so that the very law built to provide for a destitute foreigner becomes, in the story it enabled, part of the road to the Messiah's own birth. Christ is later described in exactly the kinsman redeemer role Boaz filled, the one who has both the right and the willingness to redeem those with no claim of their own.

Even the newly married man's year of exemption from war, verse 5, points forward by association. Jesus defends His disciples for not fasting by appealing to the same logic, a wedding's joy rightly interrupts ordinary demands, the guests of the bridegroom cannot mourn while He is present, Matthew 9:15. And the whole chapter's repeated ground for compassion, remember that you were slaves in Egypt, and the LORD your God redeemed you, verses 18 and 22, states in miniature the same pattern the gospel completes at full scale, redeemed people, remembering their own rescue, extending mercy to others who cannot repay them.
study.god:
The God of this chapter grounds compassion not in sentiment but in memory. Twice, at the very close of the chapter, He gives the same reason for His commands, remember that you were slaves in Egypt, and the LORD your God redeemed you from that place, verses 18 and 22. His character is not simply that He is kind, it is that His kindness has a history, and He expects His people's kindness to be shaped by having received it first, not by naturally possessing it.

He is a God who protects dignity even inside a legitimate transaction. A creditor may take security for a debt, but he may not enter a poor man's house to choose it himself, and if the pledge is something the man needs that very night, it must come back by sunset so he can sleep in his own cloak, verses 10 to 13. God does not merely permit lending, He insists that even a rightful claim be collected without humiliating the person who owes it.

He is a God of prompt, unhesitating fairness toward the powerless. A poor hired worker must be paid the same day, because he depends on that wage immediately, and the text adds a specific warning, he may cry out to the LORD against an employer who delays, and the delay itself becomes sin, verses 14 to 15. God positions Himself as the one who hears exactly that kind of unheard complaint.

He is a God of exact, individual justice rather than collective punishment. Fathers shall not be put to death for their children, nor children for their fathers, verse 16, a striking limit on the kind of corporate retribution common elsewhere in the ancient world, insisting that guilt belongs to the person who commits it.

And He is a God who builds generosity into the ordinary structure of provision rather than leaving it to occasional charity. A forgotten sheaf, the last of the olives, the last of the grapes, all of it is claimed in advance for the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow before the harvest even begins, verses 19 to 21. Compassion here is not an afterthought added once the harvest is secure, it is planned into the harvest itself, because the God who redeemed a nation of slaves does not consider provision for the vulnerable optional.

crossReferences.note: Shows this chapter's gleaning law working exactly as intended, and beyond it, when Boaz tells his workers to pull extra grain out on purpose for Ruth, a poor Moabite widow with nothing of her own.

Jesus explains that Moses permitted the certificate of divorce because your hearts were hard, not because it reflected God's original design for marriage in Genesis 2, reading this very law as a concession, not a command.

Gives the parallel gleaning command for grain and grapes, leaving the edges of a field unharvested for the poor and the foreigner, the fuller legal background this chapter's later instructions assume and then extend further.

Warns wealthy landowners that wages they have withheld from harvesters cry out and have reached the Lord of Hosts, applying this chapter's concern for prompt wages directly to New Testament economic life.

The LORD describes giving faithless Israel a certificate of divorce, the same term as Deuteronomy 24:1, an astonishing reuse of this chapter's own legal language for God's relationship with His unfaithful people.

Jesus quotes the certificate of divorce law directly before tightening its terms further, treating faithfulness in marriage as a matter of the heart rather than a procedure that a certificate alone could ever fully settle.

Amaziah spares the children of his father's assassins, explicitly citing the individual responsibility principle of Deuteronomy 24:16 as his stated reason, a rare recorded case of a king obeying Torah word for word.

Gives the same command in slightly different words, not to withhold a hired hand's wages until morning, confirming this chapter's concern for prompt payment as a standing Torah principle, not an isolated rule.

study.oneStory:
Every law in this chapter answers back to one moment Israel is told twice to remember, you were slaves in Egypt, and the LORD your God redeemed you, verses 18 and 22. That single memory is meant to explain an entire way of treating other people, a divorced woman protected in her ability to remarry, a newlywed given a year for joy, a debtor's dignity guarded even while a debt is collected, a poor laborer paid before sundown, a foreigner, a fatherless child, and a widow all guaranteed a share of the harvest before it is even gathered. None of it is arbitrary kindness, all of it flows from what God has already done for Israel and now asks Israel to extend to others.

The story this chapter belongs to runs from that redemption from Egypt toward a much larger one. Boaz's field, governed by this very gleaning law, becomes the place where a poor Moabite widow finds not just grain but a husband and a future, and her great-grandson becomes Israel's king. What the law provided as a floor of survival becomes, in one particular story, the doorway to the line that leads to the Messiah.

Even the chapter's hardest law, the certificate that legally, permanently ends a marriage, becomes material for one of Scripture's most startling pictures of God's own faithfulness. Jeremiah has the LORD describe giving faithless Israel exactly this kind of certificate, and yet the LORD does not actually let her go, He keeps calling her back. What this chapter allows a wronged husband to do, walk away for good, God refuses to do even when He has every right to.

The whole chapter, then, sits inside the Bible's larger arc from slavery to redemption to a still greater redemption. Israel was once as vulnerable as the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow this chapter protects, redeemed by a God who does not forget where His people came from. The gospel simply widens the same pattern to its true scale, a people once slaves to sin, now redeemed, freely extending to others the mercy they themselves could never have earned on their own.

quiz.q: What is the main concern of the divorce law in verses 1-4?

options.text: It forbids a man from remarrying his former wife after she has married and been divorced from, or widowed by, another man.
options.note: Verses 2-4 state this specific prohibition explicitly.

options.text: It commands every marriage to end in divorce eventually.
options.note: The text regulates an existing practice; it does not command divorce.

options.text: It requires a public trial before any divorce.
options.note: The text describes a certificate procedure, not a trial requirement.

options.text: The chapter has no teaching on divorce.
options.note: Verses 1-4 address it directly.

quiz.q: Why does the law forbid taking a millstone as security for a debt, verse 6?

options.text: Because that would be taking a person's livelihood, the means of grinding grain to live, as security.
options.note: Verse 6 gives this explicit reason.

options.text: Because millstones were too heavy to carry.
options.note: The stated reason concerns livelihood, not weight or convenience.

options.text: Because millstones were considered ceremonially unclean.
options.note: No such reason is given; the concern is economic survival.

options.text: No reason is given.
options.note: Verse 6 gives an explicit reason.

quiz.q: What must be done for a poor hired worker's wages?

options.text: He must be paid each day before sunset, since he depends on his wages and might otherwise cry out to the LORD against you.
options.note: Verses 14-15 state this explicitly.

options.text: He may be paid whenever is convenient for the employer.
options.note: The text explicitly requires same-day payment before sunset.

options.text: He should be paid once a year.
options.note: The text requires daily payment, not annual.

options.text: No instruction is given about paying workers.
options.note: Verses 14-15 are explicit.

quiz.q: According to verse 16, who bears the guilt for a person's sin?

options.text: Each person is put to death only for his own sin; fathers are not put to death for children, nor children for fathers.
options.note: Verse 16 states this explicitly.

options.text: The whole family bears guilt together for one person's sin.
options.note: Verse 16 explicitly rejects this, requiring individual accountability.

options.text: Only the eldest son bears the guilt of the family.
options.note: Verse 16 specifies each person bears his own guilt, not the eldest alone.

options.text: No teaching on guilt is given here.
options.note: Verse 16 gives explicit teaching.

quiz.q: What does the gleaning law require landowners to leave for the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow?

options.text: A forgotten sheaf, the last of the olives, and the last of the grapes, left deliberately unharvested.
options.note: Verses 19-21 state this explicitly for grain, olives, and grapes.

options.text: Nothing; the entire harvest belongs to the landowner.
options.note: Verses 19-21 explicitly require leaving a portion.

options.text: Only money, not any actual produce.
options.note: The text specifies leftover produce, not a cash provision.

options.text: The chapter gives no gleaning instructions.
options.note: Verses 19-22 give explicit gleaning instructions.

questions: Israel was told to remember its own slavery in Egypt as the reason for treating the vulnerable with compassion. What has God rescued you from that should shape how you treat someone weaker or more vulnerable than you?

A poor debtor's basic dignity, his cloak to sleep in, his livelihood, was protected even in the process of collecting what he owed. Where might you need to show more concern for a person's dignity even while holding them accountable?
Workers had to be paid promptly because they depended on their wages that day. Where do you need to be more prompt or fair in what you owe someone, whether money, time, or a promise?

The gleaning law deliberately left provision for the poor built into the ordinary rhythm of the harvest. What would it look like for you to build margin into your own life or resources for someone in need, rather than treating generosity as an afterthought?

Ruth, a foreign widow, was cared for exactly as this law intended, and became an ancestor of Christ. Where do you see God using ordinary obedience to His commands to accomplish something far bigger than you can see?

translationNotes.note: Jesus clarifies in Matthew 19:8 that this provision was a concession to hardness of heart regulating an existing practice, not a commendation of divorce or a statement of God's original design for marriage in Genesis 2:24.
'Millstone' refers to the stone used daily to grind grain into flour; taking it as loan security would deprive a poor family of the means to make their own bread, hence the explicit ban.

The gleaning law does not specify an exact percentage to leave; it functions instead as a built-in, ongoing structure of provision for the poor within Israel's agricultural economy, illustrated directly in the book of Ruth.
